Current foundation models in materials science suffer from limited generalizability, interpretability, data imbalance, safety concerns, inability to model long‑range interactions (electrostatics, dispersion, magnetism), and lack of synthesizability, phase‑stability, or safety constraints, restricting experimental feasibility of generated candidates.

The survey proposes a task‑driven taxonomy that organizes foundation models into six application areas: data extraction/interpretation/Q&A, atomistic simulation, property prediction, materials structure/design/discovery, process planning/discovery/optimization, and multiscale modeling.

LLM‑based agents such as HoneyComb, LLMatDesign, ChatMOF, MatAgent, and MatPilot have been developed to automate literature search, hypothesis generation, synthesis planning, and experimental verification in materials science.

Existing materials datasets are heavily skewed toward inorganic atomistic systems, with limited coverage of polymers, composites, and mesoscale phenomena, creating a critical data imbalance for foundation‑model training.

Future research should focus on scalable pretraining, continual learning, data governance, trustworthiness, and incorporation of physics‑informed constraints such as equivariance, quantum‑mechanical symmetries, and thermodynamic principles to improve accuracy, interpretability, and trustworthiness of foundation models.

The autonomous A‑Lab platform synthesized 41 of 58 targeted materials (71 % success) over a 17‑day experiment with minimal human intervention, demonstrating high‑throughput autonomous materials synthesis.

Benchmarks such as LLM4Mat‑Bench, MaCBench, and MatBench evaluate multiple models across millions of structures and dozens of properties, revealing significant performance differences and that domain‑specific pretraining yields substantial improvements on materials‑science tasks like property prediction and named‑entity recognition.

MatterSim, a zero‑shot machine‑learned interatomic potential trained on >17 million DFT‑labeled structures, supports universal simulation across all elements, temperatures and pressures, achieving energy prediction errors below 50 meV/atom even in high‑temperature, non‑equilibrium regimes.
SevenNet achieves over 80% parallel efficiency in weak-scaling scenarios on a 32-GPU cluster with SiO2 benchmarks.
SevenNet-0 achieves mean absolute errors of 24 meV/atom for energy, 0.067 eV/Å for force, and 0.65 GPa for stress on the test set.
The parallelization algorithm restricts communication range between neighboring processors to the original cutoff radius (rc) rather than rc multiplied by message-passing steps.
Spatial decomposition is a valid parallelization strategy only if the energy can be decomposed into atomic energies, which is key for the linear scalability of GNN-IPs.
SevenNet-0 successfully generated amorphous Si3N4 structure with 112,000 atoms through melt-quench MD simulation, reproducing key structural features matching DFT reference data.
The melt-quench simulation with 112,000 atoms on 8 GPUs demonstrated 0.94 parallel efficiency compared to single-GPU baseline.
SevenNet-0 shows improvements in energy and force accuracies compared to M3GNet (35 meV/atom, 0.072 eV/Å).
Architecture modifications reduced SevenNet-0 total model parameters from 16.24 million (GNoME) to 0.84 million.
SevenNet exhibits nearly ideal strong-scaling performance as long as GPUs are fully utilized.
Strong-scaling performance significantly declines with suboptimal GPU utilization, particularly for lightweight models or simulations with small numbers of atoms.
SevenNet-0, trained solely on crystal structures, reproduced key structural features of amorphous Si3N4 including fourfold coordination for Si and threefold coordination for N atoms.
A 60-ps MD simulation with 112,000 atoms using SevenNet-0 required 12.7 hours, approximately 0.1 ns per day.
SevenNet interfaces with the LAMMPS package for MD simulations using TorchScript to integrate trained models.
The parallelization algorithm is applicable to GNN-IP models using two-body message-passing functions including SchNet, PhysNet, PaiNN, NequIP, and MACE.
SevenNet-0 was trained on the M3GNet dataset covering 89 elements from the Materials Project database.

The DeePMD model successfully reproduces the superionic behavior of solid-state electrolytes with linear Lithium/Sodium mean squared displacement over time and diffusion coefficient uncertainty of about 20% or smaller, which is precise enough for battery applications.
The DeePMD model provides excellent energy conservation in all tested systems up to 2 ns of NVE dynamics.
For LLZO, the computed activation energies range from 0.2 to 0.22 eV, in very good agreement with experimental values of 0.20-0.21 eV for cubic LLZO.
For LGPS, the computed activation energy is 0.16 eV, which is slightly lower than experimental values (0.22 eV) but in line with previous computational studies (0.17-0.21 eV).
For NASICON, training starting from PFF-MD configurations with 480 atoms achieves convergence during the first training loop with activation energy around 0.2 eV.
For NASICON, training starting from FPMD configurations with 80 atoms fails to converge even after three training loops with activation energies spanning 0.2-0.4 eV.
Starting the training loop with PFF-MD configurations leads to faster convergence than starting with short FPMD trajectories because larger simulation cells can be used.

Training set cleaning procedures including minimum ion-ion distance cutoff, energy/force outlier removal, and loss condition monitoring are necessary to help the algorithm converge to a physical model.

The proposed training protocol based on augmenting the training set via intermediate molecular dynamics simulations can assess the quality of approximate trajectories and computed physical properties.
Starting the training loop with sufficient data sampling a relevant portion of phase space is important for obtaining generalizable models.
The DeePMD model is a promising candidate for developing a universal potential for solid-state electrolytes, though care must be taken when selecting training configurations.
For LLZO, results are quite insensitive to the choice of cell volume (NPT equilibrated vs experimental cif-file values) for producing the initial training set.
The number of force components in the initial training set is more important than total configurations for obtaining generalizable models.
MEGNet models achieve lower mean absolute errors than SchNet on 11 of the 13 QM9 molecular properties evaluated.

Simple MEGNet models that use only atomic number and spatial distance as input achieve chemical accuracy, perform comparably to full‑feature models, and outperform prior state‑of‑the‑art models on 8 of the 13 QM9 properties.

MEGNet models trained on approximately 60,000 crystals outperform prior models (SchNet and CGCNN) for formation energy, band gap, bulk modulus, and shear modulus, achieving errors comparable to or better than density‑functional‑theory uncertainties.

A unified free‑energy MEGNet model that incorporates temperature, pressure, and entropy as global state inputs predicts U₀, U, H, and G with a combined mean absolute error of 0.010 eV, comparable to separate single‑property models.

Elemental embedding vectors learned by the crystal formation‑energy MEGNet model reproduce known periodic‑table trends and, when transferred to band‑gap and elastic‑moduli models, reduce their mean absolute errors, improving upon prior machine‑learning approaches.
Ensembling two independently trained three‑block MEGNet models lowers the formation‑energy mean absolute error from 0.028 eV/atom to 0.024 eV/atom.
Increasing the number of MEGNet blocks improves accuracy for properties that depend on longer‑range interactions, such as zero‑point vibrational energy, electronic spatial extent, and dipole moment.
Graph networks constitute a universal machine‑learning framework that can accurately predict properties for both molecules and crystals.
Increasing the crystal graph radius cut‑off from 4 Å to 6 Å slightly worsens the formation‑energy mean absolute error (to 0.03 eV/atom), confirming the 4 Å cut‑off as near‑optimal.
CGAT-2 network achieves a mean absolute test error of 21 meV/atom for distance to the convex hull, enabling prediction of thermodynamic stability from unrelaxed crystal structures.
The ML-assisted high-throughput search uncovered 19,512 additional materials on the convex hull of thermodynamic stability after DFT validation.
The ML-assisted high-throughput search spanned approximately 1 billion compounds across 2500 binary and ternary structure prototypes.
Approximately 150,000 compounds were found with energy distance less than 50 meV/atom from the convex hull.
DCGAT-2 dataset contains approximately 780,000 more compounds than DCGAT-1, with 3 to 20 times more compounds containing undersampled chemical elements.
CGAT-2 shows unprecedented generalization accuracy with strongly reduced chemical and structural bias compared to previous models trained on under-represented data.
Compositional models cannot differentiate between polymorphs with the same chemical composition.
The transfer learning approach iterates until model MAE is below 30 meV/atom.
Out of 50 materials screened for electron-phonon calculations, 19 systems were found with Tc above 1 K, with ScMoC2 having the highest transition temperature at 15.97 K.
The ternary compound TiVB3 is predicted to have a superhard hardness of 42 GPa.
338 extreme materials were identified from predicted deformation potentials for full deformation potential calculation.
Materials within 50 meV/atom from convex hull were selected for subsequent DFT stiffness tensor calculations.

A graph convolutional neural network predicts vibrational free energies with root‑mean‑square errors of 8.23 meV/atom (training), 11.34 meV/atom (validation) and 12.31 meV/atom (test), and its predictions for MgS and NaH polymorphs match DFT‑computed values across the 200–700 K range.

Screening of approximately 50 000 inorganic crystals with the machine‑learning model identified over 2 000 temperature‑induced solid‑solid polymorphic transitions between 300 K and 600 K, including 130 stable transitions within the technologically relevant 300 K–350 K interval.

Twenty‑one stable polar‑nonpolar transitions are predicted to exhibit relative lattice‑thermal‑conductivity changes of at least 20 % (0.20), ranging up to a 73 % increase for ZrSeO with a conductivity ratio of 1.73.

Several predicted solid‑solid transitions show large entropy changes exceeding 300 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹ (e.g., Li₃MnF₇: 342.3 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹, PnCl₂: 338.3 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹, Fe₄OF₇: 252.1 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹), while the highest entropy changes (> 400 J K⁻¹ kg⁻¹) are limited to transitions above 450 K and occur exclusively in nonpolar‑nonpolar categories, reducing their relevance for room‑temperature applications.

The presented workflow enables high‑throughput prediction of temperature‑induced solid‑solid phase transitions without performing explicit phonon calculations for each material, dramatically reducing computational cost.

Validation against experimental reports and independent first‑principles calculations confirms the robustness and predictive power of the ML‑guided framework, with reasonable agreement for transition temperatures of KNO₃, KNO₂ and CaCO₃, DFT‑calculated free‑energy differences matching ML predictions for a ten‑material subset, and thermal‑conductivity ratios for Li₄TiS₄ and NaNO₃ closely reproduced by DFT.

Uncertainty quantification based on latent‑space Euclidean distance provides error estimates that correlate with prediction errors, allowing exclusion of transitions whose uncertainty exceeds 50 % of the absolute free‑energy difference.

Polar‑nonpolar and polar‑polar transitions are more numerous than nonpolar‑nonpolar ones, with 214 polar‑nonpolar, 173 polar‑polar and 228 nonpolar‑nonpolar stable transitions predicted in the 300 K–600 K range.
Metastable phase transitions outnumber stable transitions across all symmetry categories in the screened dataset.
Across the screened temperature range, a larger number of predicted stable phase transitions is generally associated with smaller phase‑transition entropy changes.
The current screening neglects thermal‑expansion effects, which may cause discrepancies with experimental transition temperatures, especially when expansion strongly influences phase stability.

The atomic cluster expansion (ACE) is generalized to model scalar, vectorial and tensorial atomic properties and to include additional atomic degrees of freedom—species, magnetic moments, and charges—on equal footing with atomic positions.
The derived ACE formulas enable efficient evaluation of forces and magnetic torques.
At the lowest order, the magnetic ACE reproduces a distance‑dependent Heisenberg interaction.

Representing tensors with spherical harmonics yields a dramatically sparser basis, where a rank‑N Cartesian tensor with 3^N components can be represented by (N+1)^2 spherical harmonics (e.g., a 10th‑order tensor requires 121 harmonics instead of 59 049 Cartesian components).
Moments Tensor Potentials (MTP) and the Spectral Neighbor Analysis Potential (SNAP) can be expressed exactly as special cases of the ACE.

Neglecting spin‑orbit coupling forces all magnetic angular momenta to be zero, greatly reducing the number of ACE expansion coefficients, since the magnetic contribution to the cohesive energy is only about 10 % of the total.
The ACE formulation is invariant under translation, rotation, inversion and permutation of identical atoms.
Although the full magnetic and charge‑transfer ACE contains many parameters, hierarchical ordering of interactions allows robust and systematic fitting to reference data.
Implementing the extended ACE for vectorial, tensorial, magnetic and charge degrees of freedom requires no significantly greater effort than the original scalar ACE implementation.
Because the ACE basis is complete and hierarchical, it can in principle achieve arbitrary accuracy for any scalar, vectorial or tensorial property.

EquiformerV2+DeNS (a universal interatomic potential) achieves the highest classification performance among all evaluated models, with F1 scores up to 0.983, ROC AUC 0.96, and discovery acceleration factors up to 6.33, establishing state‑of‑the‑art for ML‑guided materials discovery.

Training universal interatomic potential models with forces, stresses, and magnetic moments substantially improves stability‑prediction performance compared with energy‑only models, enhancing both classification metrics (F1, DAF) and regression metrics (MAE, RMSE).

Regression‑based metrics such as MAE, RMSE, and R² are poorly aligned with classification‑based metrics needed for materials‑discovery tasks, and improvements in these regression metrics do not necessarily translate into higher F1 or discovery acceleration scores.

The WBM test set contains 215,488 unique prototype structures (32,942 thermodynamically stable), is enriched in actinides, lanthanides, metalloids and noble‑transition metals while under‑representing oxygen, is dominated by ternary phases (~75 %), and most structures have fewer than 100 atomic sites, contrasting with the Materials Project training distribution.

Prospective benchmarking that introduces covariate shift between training and test distributions provides a more realistic indicator of real‑world discovery performance than retrospective split strategies, and requires training and test sets larger than the training set to evaluate model scalability.
Random‑forest models excel on small datasets but are outperformed by neural‑network models on large datasets due to the benefits of representation learning.
Optimizing hyperparameters solely for the Matbench Discovery benchmark may degrade performance of models intended for general‑purpose use.
Models trained on Materials Project data systematically underpredict convex‑hull distances because the training set is biased toward low‑formation‑energy (stable) structures.
High disagreement among model predictions (large standard deviation) can be used to flag potential DFT relaxation failures in high‑throughput screenings.
Accurate regression models can still produce high false‑positive rates near the 0 eV/atom convex‑hull decision boundary.

Using the MACE checkpoint trained on the M3GNet dataset caused volume implosion failures for several hundred of the 250 k test crystals, whereas the checkpoint trained on the MPtrj dataset reduced failures to only 44 crystals.

Extrapolation performance degrades with increasing WBM batch number for most models, especially Wrenformer and Voronoi RF, while universal interatomic potential models (e.g., EquiformerV2, ORB) show minimal degradation across batches.

GNoME discovered 2.2 million crystal structures stable with respect to the Materials Project, with 381,000 newly on the convex hull, representing an order-of-magnitude expansion from all previous discoveries.
736 GNoME-discovered structures match experimentally validated ICSD structures, with 184 representing novel discoveries since the project began.

GNoME achieves hit rates above 80% for structural predictions and 33% for composition-only predictions, compared to 1% in previous work, with active learning improving from less than 6% and 3% respectively over six rounds.
Final GNoME models predict energies with a mean absolute error of 11 meV per atom on relaxed structures, improved from 21 meV per atom in the initial model trained on Materials Project data.

GNNs trained on large and diverse first-principles calculations increase the number of stable crystals by more than an order of magnitude, with scaling showing consistent power-law improvements in MLIP accuracy and generalization on out-of-distribution structural tasks.

Large-scale pretraining of MLIPs on GNoME dataset enables models with unprecedented zero-shot accuracy on downstream AIMD data, outperforming state-of-the-art NequIP models trained on hundreds of structures from the target distribution.
GNoME discovered crystals correspond to 45,500 novel prototypes, a 5.6x increase from the 8,000 in Materials Project.
GNoME discovers approximately 52,000 layered materials compared to approximately 1,000 in Materials Project, and finds 528 promising Li-ion conductors, a 25x increase compared to the original study.
GNoME enables efficient discovery of materials with 4+ unique elements, which have been difficult for previous discovery efforts.

More than 10⁹ candidate structures were generated over the course of active learning using symmetry-aware partial substitutions and random structure search, with 232,477 out of 381,000 stable structures (approximately 61%) attributed to the SAPS candidate generation procedure.
GNoME-driven molecular dynamics simulations on 623 materials with previously unseen compositions enable classification of unseen compositions as superionic conductors in comparison with AIMD.

Crystal structures, data, and software for analyzing stable crystals, phase diagrams, static GNN, and interatomic potentials will be made available at the Google DeepMind materials_discovery GitHub repository and via the Materials Project with permanent DOI link 10.17188/2009989.
Previous machine-learning techniques have been ineffective in estimating material stability (decomposition energy) with respect to the convex hull.
GNoME discovered 381,000 new stable crystal structures on the convex hull, far exceeding the 13,000 new stable crystals discovered by external research efforts from 2021 to 2023.
91% of 2,202 new Materials Project compositions added since the snapshot match GNoME database on structure.
The GNN predicts atomic von Mises stress in polycrystalline graphene with a mean normalized relative error of 5.5% and a maximum error below 7% on a test set of 400 crystals.
The GNN predicts atomic tensile stress in porous graphene membranes under tensile strain with a mean normalized relative error of 4.9% and a maximum error of about 10%.
The GNN reproduces the linear decrease of Young’s modulus with vacancy concentration in porous graphene, matching MD results and yielding the fitted relation E = 823.7 − 5635.6·Cv (GPa).

In polycrystalline aluminum, the GNN predicts atomic potential energy with a mean normalized relative error of 11.0% (maximum ≈13%) and achieves R² = 0.99 for mean potential energy versus grain number.
Including tensile strain as an input node feature enables the GNN to accurately predict stress evolution during loading, reproducing nonlinear strain‑stress curves for porous graphene.
The GNN’s stress predictions are substantially more accurate than on‑the‑fly stress calculations from the force field, which exhibit higher errors.

The GNN framework generalizes across defect types (grain boundaries, vacancies) and material dimensionalities (2D graphene, 3D aluminum), and to unseen defect configurations in over 10⁶ porous graphene structures, maintaining high prediction accuracy despite being trained on only about 1,200 random samples.

Coupling the GNN with a genetic algorithm efficiently discovers optimal holey graphene designs (e.g., arrow‑shaped hole patterns) that achieve significantly lower stress concentration than suboptimal designs, using only ~800 stress evaluations—an order of magnitude fewer than brute‑force search—and reliably locates the global minimum in most of 1,000 random initializations.

The GNN respects physical constraints, accurately capturing derivative properties such as stress fields that obey underlying physical laws, and predicts global properties (Young’s modulus, total potential energy) that follow known physical relationships and match MD results across different crystalline systems.

The Principal Neighbourhood Aggregation (PNA) GNN model achieves the lowest mean and variance of test mean‑squared error among GCN, GAT, and MPNN (sum and max) variants on the polycrystalline graphene dataset.
The GNN accelerates atomic property prediction by hundreds to thousands of times compared with conventional MD simulations, requiring seconds on a single CPU versus thousands of seconds on 24 CPUs.

Linear fitting of atomic properties yields substantially higher prediction errors than the GNN approach, demonstrating the superiority of the nonlinear GNN model for mapping initial structures to final property distributions.

DeePMD reproduces AIMD energies, forces, and virial tensors for water and ice with root‑mean‑square errors of approximately 1 meV per molecule for energy, 40 meV Å⁻¹ for forces, and 1–2 meV for the virial.
DeePMD accurately reproduces radial distribution functions and three‑body angular distribution functions of liquid water and ice, matching AIMD results.
For a diverse set of organic molecules, DeePMD achieves lower mean absolute errors in both energy and forces than the GDML benchmark.
The computational cost of DeePMD scales linearly with the number of atoms and is several orders of magnitude lower than equivalent AIMD simulations, comparable to empirical force fields.
A DeePMD model trained on relatively small systems (64–96 water or ice molecules) can be directly applied to much larger systems without loss of accuracy, demonstrating strong transferability.
DeePMD preserves translational, rotational, and permutational symmetries by constructing a local reference frame for each atom and sorting neighbor lists by species and inverse distance.
Using a loss function with adaptive prefactors that emphasize forces early and energies/virial later reduces the total training time to a few core‑hours for all test cases.
Discontinuities in forces caused by the sharp cutoff radius and neighbor‑list sorting are much smaller than thermal fluctuations and do not impair canonical sampling.
In principle, DeePMD could be trained on chemically accurate data from high‑level quantum chemistry or quantum Monte Carlo, extending its applicability beyond density‑functional theory.
DeepH-E3 provides a universal E(3)-equivariant deep-learning framework that exactly preserves Euclidean symmetry of the DFT Hamiltonian, including spin-orbit coupling.

DeepH-E3 predicts DFT Hamiltonian matrix elements with sub‑meV mean absolute error, reducing the error by roughly a factor of two compared with the original DeepH method across diverse material systems.

DeepH-E3 enables accurate electronic‑structure calculations for supercells larger than 10⁴ atoms, reducing computational cost by several orders of magnitude and allowing calculations in minutes on a single GPU versus months on thousands of CPU cores.

DeepH‑E3 reproduces the band structure of magic‑angle twisted bilayer graphene (θ = 1.08°, 11 164 atoms) in excellent agreement with DFT and low‑energy continuum models, correctly capturing the flat bands near the Fermi level.

DeepH‑E3 predicts a spin‑orbit‑coupling‑induced topological quantum phase transition in twisted bilayer Bi₂Te₃, evidenced by band‑gap closing and reopening and a change of the Z₂ invariant from 0 to 1 as SOC strength increases.
DeepH‑E3 attains sub‑meV accuracy after training on only a few hundred DFT calculations of small, non‑twisted structures, demonstrating high data efficiency.
DeepH‑E3 generalizes across diverse material systems—including graphene, MoS₂, bismuthene, Bi₂Se₃, and Bi₂Te₃—achieving consistently sub‑meV Hamiltonian prediction errors.
The model generalizes to arbitrarily twisted bilayer structures; the mean absolute error of Hamiltonian predictions decreases as the Moiré supercell size grows (or twist angle decreases).

The equivariant architecture handles spin‑orbital Hamiltonians by separating real and imaginary components and applying a change‑of‑basis for half‑integer representations, thereby preserving equivariance without requiring complex‑valued network layers.
The model can fit 2.8 × 10⁹ non‑zero complex‑valued Hamiltonian matrix elements with only ~10⁵ real trainable parameters, indicating high capacity efficiency.
EquiformerV2 outperforms state-of-the-art methods on OC20 and OC22 datasets, improving upon eSCN by 4-9% on force MAE and 4-18.9% on energy MAE.
EquiformerV2 trained on only OC22 (8.4M structures) achieves better results than GemNet-OC trained on both OC20 (130M structures) and OC22, demonstrating significantly better data efficiency.

EquiformerV2 can scale Lmax to 6 or 8 on OC20 dataset using eSCN convolutions that reduce computational cost from O(L^6) to O(L^3), whereas original Equiformer is impractical for Lmax > 2 on large-scale datasets.

EquiformerV2 offers better speed-accuracy trade-offs than Equiformer, being 2.3x faster at Lmax=2 while achieving better force MAE, and requiring 1.4x less training time when increasing Lmax from 2 to 4.

EquiformerV2 incorporates three architectural improvements: attention re-normalization, separable S2 activation, and separable layer normalization, replacing SO(3) convolutions with eSCN convolutions to efficiently incorporate higher-degree tensors.
EquiformerV2 achieves the highest success rate in the AdsorbML algorithm and enables a 2x reduction in DFT calculations needed for computing adsorption energies.
EquiformerV2 achieves better results than Equiformer on 9 out of 12 tasks on the QM9 dataset and is the overall best performing model.
Higher degree representations (larger Lmax) better capture angular resolution and directional information critical for accurate force prediction and correlate with model expressivity.
eSCN convolutions reduce SO(3) tensor product complexity by replacing non-trivial paths with SO(2) linear operations while maintaining equivariance.
Attention re-normalization improves energy MAE by 2.4% while force MAE remains approximately the same.

Separable S2 activation prevents large gradients by separating activation for degree 0 and degree > 0 vectors, whereas directly replacing gate activation with S2 activation causes training instability and non-convergence.
Separable Layer Normalization preserves relative magnitudes between degrees > 0, improving performance over independent degree normalization.
MACE uses four-body (higher-order) messages, allowing only two message‑passing layers to achieve converged accuracy, whereas prior equivariant MPNNs required five or six layers.
MACE attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy, achieving lower root‑mean‑square energy and force errors than previous models on the rMD17, 3BPA, and AcAc benchmark suites.

MACE evaluates roughly ten times faster than prior force‑field models for invariant (L=0) architectures and 4–5 times faster for equivariant (L=1,2) architectures, while delivering lower prediction errors.

MACE shows superior extrapolation ability, reducing energy RMSE by about 30 % at 1200 K and 40 % on dihedral‑slice energies for the 3BPA benchmark, and achieving lower errors on geometries far from the training distribution.
On the 3BPA molecule energy profile, MACE predictions are closest to the DFT ground truth across three dihedral slices, outperforming BOTNet and NequIP.
MACE reaches high accuracy rapidly, matching a converged BOTNet model on the 3BPA dataset after roughly 30 minutes of training on an NVIDIA A100 GPU, and trains each benchmark dataset in 2–6 hours.

The computational cost of MACE scales O(1) with the number of chemical elements because species embeddings are continuous and not included in the tensor‑product contraction, and higher‑order features are implemented via an efficient single‑loop tensor‑contraction algorithm.
By decoupling body‑order from the number of message‑passing iterations, MACE has a small receptive field of approximately 4–5 Å per layer, enabling efficient parallelisation across GPUs.
Increasing the correlation order of messages (ν) steepens the learning‑curve power law, yielding higher data efficiency.
Virtual Node Graph Neural Network (VGNN) enables graph neural networks to handle variable output dimensions by incorporating virtual nodes that resemble phonon dynamical matrices.

Three virtual node approaches were developed: vector virtual nodes (VVN) outputting 3m Γ-phonon branches, matrix virtual nodes (MVN) with m² 3×3 matrices, and momentum-dependent matrix virtual nodes (k-MVN) for full band structure prediction.
VGNN achieves direct prediction of Γ-phonon spectra and full phonon dispersion using only atomic coordinates as input without prior knowledge of interatomic forces.
VGNN-based phonon calculation achieves significantly faster computation speed than ab initio methods (DFPT, frozen-phonon) while maintaining reasonable accuracy.
Computing Γ-phonon spectra for 146,323 Materials Project materials took less than five hours on an eight-GPU system, even for materials with over 400 atoms per unit cell.
MVN outperforms VVN for Γ-phonon prediction, especially for complex materials, at the cost of slightly higher computational expense.
The k-MVN method can predict full phonon band structures at arbitrary k points in the Brillouin zone by incorporating momentum dependence through phase factors for unit-cell translations.
The approach generalizes to materials with varying atom counts, tested on systems with 2–40 atoms (training) and over 40 atoms (testing).
The k-MVN model can handle phonon prediction for alloys ranging from binary to five-component high entropy alloys by encoding atomic composition through weighted atomic masses.
A Γ-phonon database containing phonon spectra for 146,323 Materials Project materials was generated using the MVN approach, with unit cell atom counts ranging from 1 to 444 atoms.
The model was trained on a DFPT computational database containing phonon dispersion data for 1,521 crystalline inorganic materials.
For very complicated materials, VVN-predicted phonons tend to have higher frequencies than ground truth, and prediction loss becomes larger as input materials become more complicated.
Phonon bandstructures were validated on various alloy systems including SiGe, FeCoNi, and other high-energy alloys with agreement to existing literature.
While exact phonon band matching with DFPT is not always achieved, the model captures key features such as average frequency and band gaps.
The Γ-phonon database exhibits a hyperbolic relationship between average frequency and average atomic mass following ω̄ = C m̄^(-1/2) with C ≈ 1993.

UMA models are trained on approximately 500 million unique 3D atomic structures (459M training examples with over 30 billion atoms) across five domains, representing the largest training runs to date for atomic models and covering nearly the entire chemical space except radioactive elements.

The Mixture of Linear Experts (MoLE) architecture enables increasing model capacity without sacrificing inference speed, with a compute-optimal MoLE model achieving equivalent validation loss to dense models using approximately 2.5× fewer active parameters.
UMA sets new state-of-the-art performance on Matbench Discovery and AdsorbML benchmarks, with UMA-M achieving the highest F1 score to date (0.929) on Matbench Discovery.
UMA-M reduces OC20 S2EF adsorption energy prediction errors by approximately 80% compared to previous state-of-the-art models, achieving 33.4 meV MAE versus 149.1 meV for EquiformerV2-OC20.
UMA models conserve energy in NVE molecular dynamics simulations across all tested configurations spanning materials and molecules benchmarks.
UMA-S can simulate 1,000 atoms at 16 steps per second (1.4ns per day) and fit system sizes up to 100,000+ atoms in memory on a single 80GB GPU.
A single UMA model without any fine-tuning performs similarly or better than task-specialized models across diverse DFT tasks including materials, catalysis, molecules, molecular crystals, and MOFs.
A novel two-stage training schedule with BF16 pre-training followed by FP32 fine-tuning recovers the 20-50% accuracy loss from BF16 precision alone while enabling efficient training.
UMA models achieve sub-20 meV/atom energy MAE on multiple molecule benchmarks including biomolecules and electrolytes, and lattice energy prediction accuracy of ≤3 kJ/mol for molecular crystals.
UMA models demonstrate log-linear scaling behavior at compute scales of 10^18-10^20 FLOPs, indicating greater model capacity is required to fit the UMA dataset.
Multi-task UMA models do not overfit to forces during training, unlike single-task models which frequently exhibit force overfitting.
UMA-M achieves ligand strain errors approaching DFT reference accuracy, demonstrating practical surrogate capability for structure-based drug design applications.
Combined graph parallelism, fully-sharded data parallelism, and activation checkpointing enables reliable scaling of UMA model training up to 10B total parameters.
Moving from 1 to 8 experts yields significant loss improvement in MoLE models, while gains from 32 to 128 experts are negligible.
Scaling law experiments were only performed on pretraining due to compute constraints, without studying finetuning effects with energy conservation.

The final M3GNet interatomic potential achieves test mean absolute errors of 0.035 eV/atom for energy, 0.072 eV/Å for forces, and 0.41 GPa for stresses on a held‑out Materials Project dataset covering 89 elements.
Relaxing test crystals with M3GNet reduces median volume error from 2.4 % to 0.6 % and energy mean absolute error from 0.169 eV/atom to 0.035 eV/atom relative to DFT‑relaxed references.

A single‑CPU M3GNet relaxation completes in about 22 seconds, compared with 15 hours on 32 cores for DFT; pre‑relaxation with M3GNet shortens subsequent DFT relaxation time by roughly a factor of three and reduces total CPU time by an average factor of 2.97.

Screening 31.7 million hypothetical crystals with M3GNet identifies approximately 1.8 million candidates with predicted hull distances below 0.001 eV/atom, and among the 2,000 lowest‑energy candidates, 1,578 are confirmed stable (Ehull < 0.001 eV/atom) by DFT.

Training M3GNet on energies alone (M3GNet‑E) yields force and stress mean absolute errors larger than the intrinsic data dispersion, demonstrating that forces and stresses must be included in training.
A single universal M3GNet model trained simultaneously on six elements attains error metrics comparable to element‑specific M3GNet models.

M3GNet predicts phonon band structures and densities of states for SiO₂ polymorphs that quantitatively agree with DFT calculations, and the predicted phonon density‑of‑states center follows the expected ω ∝ 1/√m trend across materials.

M3GNet molecular‑dynamics simulations of Li₃YCl₆ reproduce ionic conductivity (14.3 mS cm⁻¹) and activation energy (0.22 eV) consistent with ab‑initio MD, and short‑time MD correctly identifies known lithium superionic conductors by their high mean‑squared displacements at elevated temperatures.

On the MD17 and MD17‑CCSD(T) molecular force‑field benchmarks, M3GNet achieves lower energy and force errors than the Embedded Atom Neural Network and comparable accuracy to state‑of‑the‑art message‑passing and equivariant neural networks; when benchmarked against quantum‑accurate CCSD/CCSD(T) data, it attains state‑of‑the‑art accuracy for several molecules.

Across nine MatBench structural property datasets, M3GNet yields lower mean absolute errors than MODNet, AtomSets‑V1, MEGNet, and AutoMatminer, with improvements of 20.5 %–41.3 % on large datasets such as perovskite formation energy and MP band gap, and demonstrates excellent prediction accuracy on the broader MatBench suite.

For a MgO test set, M3GNet outperforms Moment Tensor Potentials in extrapolating equation‑of‑state behavior beyond the training regime and exhibits long‑range interaction characteristics similar to a Buckingham + Coulomb model.
The M3GNet architecture preserves continuity of energies, forces, and stresses with respect to changes in bond count, satisfying a necessary physical constraint for interatomic potentials.

The Open Quantum Materials Database (OQMD) contains over 200,000 DFT‑calculated crystal structures, including experimental ICSD entries and theoretical prototype structures, and is freely accessible to the scientific community without usage restrictions.
At 0 K and zero pressure, 23 % of the 32,489 ICSD structures in the OQMD are thermodynamically stable according to grand canonical linear programming analysis.
The average error between DFT‑predicted formation energies in the OQMD and experimental values from the SGTE database is 24 meV/atom, with a mean absolute error of 113 meV/atom.
High‑throughput screening identified TiP, LiSiNi₂, and CoSi₂ as the most promising Li‑ion battery anode conversion reactions, offering high capacity, moderate voltage, and low volume expansion.

Among binary metal‑oxide candidates, Al₂O₃ provides the optimal balance of HF‑scavenging tendency, lithiation voltage, gravimetric and volumetric capacities, outperforming other oxides in the four‑dimensional design space.
All eleven experimentally known rare‑earth‑containing Mg‑XL‑XS LPSO systems are correctly predicted to be thermodynamically stable by DFT calculations using OQMD convex hulls.
DFT screening predicts forty‑one previously unreported rare‑earth‑containing Mg‑XL‑XS ternary systems to be thermodynamically stable LPSO phases, providing new experimental targets.

Calcium and strontium are predicted to form stable (or nearly stable) LPSO precipitates in Mg alloys, offering affordable alternatives to rare‑earth elements, with Ca especially promising in the Mg‑Ca‑Zn system.

A combined heuristic‑plus‑machine‑learning model trained on OQMD ternary formation energies predicts formation energies with a mean absolute error of ~0.11 eV/atom, roughly half the typical DFT‑experiment error.

Applying the heuristic‑ML model to 1.6 million hypothetical ternary compositions identified nine top candidates, of which eight were confirmed by DFT to be new stable compounds (e.g., SiYb₃F₅, Pa₂O(SiO₆)).
AFLOW can automatically calculate a wide suite of physical observables across a large database of structures with minimal human intervention.

AFLOW detects most calculation failures, automatically corrects input parameters, restarts calculations, and can run as a Unix daemon to generate, run, correct, and converge many DFT jobs per day, yielding higher throughput than manual management.
AFLOW provides a standardized definition of Brillouin‑zone integration paths for all 14 Bravais lattices, filling a gap in the literature.
AFLOW reproduces experimental phonon dispersion curves for face‑centered cubic Rhodium, showing excellent agreement with measured data.

AFLOW’s cage‑finding algorithm identifies interstitial sites via a topological method, finding 14 cages (6 octahedral, 8 tetrahedral) that reduce to 5 symmetrically inequivalent positions, with radii of 2.2225 Å (octahedral) and 1.9248 Å (tetrahedral).
AFLOW can automatically generate high‑index surface slabs for complex multicomponent compounds, demonstrated for (001), (110) and (111) slabs of an fcc L10 binary.
AFLOW can automatically create nanoparticle structures of arbitrary radius and separation, enabling high‑throughput nanoparticle studies.
AFLOW can automatically construct convex hulls for binary alloy systems at zero temperature using formation enthalpies from DFT calculations.
The AFLOW database currently contains approximately 400 experimental prototype structures and several million bcc/fcc/hcp‑derived superstructures.
A hybrid HSE06 calculation for ZnO yields a band gap of 2.48 eV, substantially larger than the LDA/GGA gap of 0.7 eV and the PBE+U gap of 1.82 eV.
Tuning the exact‑exchange fraction α to 0.375 in HSE06 brings the calculated ZnO band gap into agreement with experiment.
Hybrid functional calculations scale approximately as O(N^2.5) for small systems and linearly beyond ~15 Å (HSE06) or ~100 Å (PBE0), whereas standard GGA calculations scale as O(N^3).
AFLOW implements DFT+U using the Dudarev formalism with default Ueff values for a wide range of elements.
A bulk ZnO HSE06 calculation (8×8×6 k‑point mesh, 400 eV cutoff) takes approximately 5 hours on 8 CPUs, while the equivalent GGA/PBE+U calculation finishes in less than a minute.
AFLOW can predict alloy miscibility using Miedema and Hume‑Rothery mixing rules.
The Gaussian approximation potential (GAP) enables atomistic simulations with close-to-DFT accuracy at computational costs many orders of magnitude lower than quantum-mechanical methods.

Combined two-body, three-body, and SOAP many-body descriptors are necessary for GAP to achieve the accuracy limit imposed by force locality and make physically meaningful predictions; models using only subsets of descriptors produce unphysical structures during molecular dynamics simulations.

GAP predicts diamond lattice parameter (3.539 Å) very close to DFT-LDA reference (3.532 Å), outperforming screened Tersoff potential (3.566 Å), with bulk modulus and elastic constants reasonably close to DFT reference values.
GAP radial and angular distribution functions for liquid and amorphous carbon closely match DFT reference results, including peak locations, extents, and overall curve shapes.
GAP recovers three- and four-membered rings that are key features of liquid and low-density amorphous carbon structures, which empirical potentials (Tersoff/Brenner) fail to predict.
GAP fully reproduces the stability ordering of ta-C surface energies compared to DFT calculations, with differences less than 0.01 J m−2 for the most stable surface.

GAP predictions for Young's modulus of amorphous carbon agree very well with experimental values at all relevant densities, while screened Tersoff potential captures the trend but significantly overestimates absolute values.

GAP sp3 concentration predictions are closer to DFT reference than empirical Brenner and Tersoff potentials, particularly at lower densities; empirical potentials underestimate sp3 concentration in tetrahedral amorphous carbon.

Empirical potentials (Tersoff/Brenner) cannot describe interlayer spacing in graphite due to short-range cutoff being less than c/2, provide poor description of carbon surfaces, and yield much lower surface energies than GAP and DFT for ta-C surfaces.
Diamond exhibits strong force locality with force deviations vanishing practically at rfix = 5.5 Å, while graphite is highly nonlocal with larger force deviations that do not decay as rapidly.

For amorphous carbon with 3.7 Å cutoff radius, the lowest achievable standard deviation of force components is approximately 1 eV/Å due to fundamental nonlocality limits, representing a maximum accuracy bound for any finite-range interatomic potential.

DFT-based methods are practically limited to systems of a few hundred atoms, making generation of 8,000-atom amorphous carbon structures impossible with DFT-MD even on state-of-the-art supercomputers.

All fitting coefficients in the GAP model enter linearly, allowing solution via simple linear algebra rather than difficult nonlinear parameter optimization required for traditional potentials and neural networks.

The training database includes liquid and amorphous structures, randomly distorted crystalline allotropes (diamond and graphite), and isolated dimer DFT data, extended iteratively by performing melt-quench simulations driven by previous GAP versions with DFT single-point computations for validation snapshots.
GAP predicts graphite c parameter at 6.518 Å versus 6.625 Å from DFT, representing -1.6% overbinding.
